name: Daytona
oneLiner: Firecracker VMs with custom sizes, per-second billing and a 24-hour session cap, sold per core with a desktop, a Mac reservation and no stop button on Linux.
whatItIs: Daytona 2.0 sells sandboxes for AI agents: a Linux Firecracker microVM by default, a Windows or GPU Cloud Hypervisor VM, or a macOS VM on a reserved Apple Mac. Every sandbox is created, driven and deleted through Python and TypeScript SDKs, a CLI, a REST API, an MCP server and a dashboard.

The 2.0 model is task-shaped. Sizes are custom from 0.125 to 16 cores and 0.5 to 32 GiB, the disk is free ephemeral NVMe, and a sandbox runs until its idle or wall-clock timeout deletes it. Linux has no stop, pause or fork; keeping files between sessions means a volume, and keeping a running process means a snapshot or an image.

It is the second platform from the same company. Daytona 1.x at daytona.io is still sold, still documented as v0.231 Latest, and still runs containers; 2.0 is a VM-first rebuild, labelled v2.0 Alpha in the 1.x docs, with alpha clients and an import path for archived 1.x sandboxes.
whoFor: Teams building coding, browser or computer-use agents who want a real VM per task, are happy to recreate it from an image or volume, and need macOS or Windows next to Linux.
isolation: Every sandbox is a hardware-isolated VM with its own kernel: Linux on Firecracker, Windows and GPU on Cloud Hypervisor, macOS on Apple's Virtualization framework. The hypervisor enforces the boundary. Docker runs only when the image ships Docker Engine; nested virtualisation (/dev/kvm) is Enterprise-only.
sizes: Custom: 0.125 to 16 cores, 0.5 to 32 GiB memory, 10 to 256 GiB disk, with CPU raised to at least 1 core per 8 GiB. Plan caps are 4 cores / 16 GiB on Starter and 8 / 32 on Team (the pricing page advertises 64 / 128). Default 0.5 cores, 1 GiB memory and 512 MiB disk. A macOS sandbox takes 4 to 12 cores, 4 to 24 GiB and 80 to 220 GiB from a Mac reservation. Regions: earth (1.0×), us (1.15×), us-east (1.75×), us-east-ash-1 and us-east-bos-1 (2.0×), plus macos-1.

billing.model: Per-second metered billing on guaranteed cores, memory and disk, with a measured burst above the guarantee up to the limit. Starter is pay-as-you-go; Team adds $250 a month; Enterprise is custom.
billing.meter: CPU $0.101 per core-hour ($0.0505 per vCPU-hour where a core is 2 vCPUs), memory $0.0162 per GiB-hour, ephemeral NVMe $0, volumes $0.000108 per GiB-hour, Windows $0.172 per core-hour, macOS a $2.5032 per Mac-hour reservation, GPUs $0.99 to $8.99 per GPU-hour. Spot is 0.7 times; CPU types multiply by 1.0, 1.6667 or 2.3313; regions by 1.0 to 2.0.
billing.stopped: A stopped or paused sandbox is not metered for CPU, memory or disk, and a deleted one bills only its volumes. Linux cannot stop or pause, so it bills its guarantee until deleted. A paused macOS sandbox keeps paying its Mac reservation.
billing.planFee: $0 on Starter, $250 a month on Team with $100 of credits that expire at the end of the billing period, custom on Enterprise.
billing.minimum: $200 one-time credit on Starter with no card. No recurring free tier. The minimum wallet top-up is $10.

A.headline: $27.63 a month
A.shape: 2 vCPU / 4 GiB / 10 GiB (1 core), deleted after each task
notes: 2 vCPU is 1 core only where SMT is on; on Graviton or Apple silicon it is 2 cores and $0.202 an hour, or $33.67 a month.
The 10 GiB disk is ephemeral NVMe at $0.000/GiB-hour, so it adds nothing.
The $200 Starter credit covers 7.2 months of this workload.
Spot is 30% cheaper ($19.34) but can be reclaimed mid-task.

B.headline: $246.01 a month
B.shape: 4 vCPU / 8 GiB / 50 GiB (2 cores) plus a 50 GiB volume, 730 h
notes: The 50 GiB ephemeral disk is free; the volume is what keeps the files across the 24-hour session cap, and it bills from byte one.
Without the volume the bill is $242.07, but the files go when the session ends.
On spot the same box is $172.21 and can be reclaimed without warning.
B.flag: A 730-hour session exceeds Starter's 24-hour and Team's 48-hour cap: the sandbox must be recreated from an image or with its volume about 30 times a month (15 on Team).

C.headline: $16.50 a month
C.shape: 2 vCPU / 4 GiB / 20 GiB (1 core) plus a 20 GiB volume, 90 h running
notes: A Linux sandbox cannot stop: the 640 idle hours are a deleted sandbox with its disk on a volume, not a paused one.
Left running for the whole month instead, the same shape costs $121.03; the volume is what makes C cheap.
The volume bills for all 730 hours, including the 90 the sandbox is running.

facts.label: Legal entity

facts.label: Scale
facts.value: The CEO reports a $1M to $100M run rate in four quarters, 37.5x growth this year. Self-reported; not audited.

source.quote: That is how long it took us to go from a $1M run rate to $100M.

facts.label: Status page
facts.value: A public Better Stack status page with per-component uptime; all services were online at the check. It is shared with 1.x and does not separate the two platforms.

facts.label: SLA
facts.value: 99.95% monthly availability, under an SLA last updated 22 August 2025. Service credits are limited to Tier 4 and above, a 1.x tier with no 2.0 plan of that name (see the caveat).

source.quote: Daytona will use commercially reasonable efforts to make the Services available 99.95% of the time in any given calendar month

facts.label: Certification
facts.value: The trust centre lists SOC 2 Type 1, SOC 2 Type 2, HIPAA, GDPR and ISO/IEC 27001, and offers a pentest report on request.

facts.label: Data processing
facts.value: A public DPA with EU standard contractual clauses governed by Irish law, a subprocessor list, and email notice of subprocessor changes.

source.quote: the EU SCCs will be governed by the laws of Ireland

facts.label: Price changes
facts.value: No notice period: fees may change by posting the change on the service. The Terms also say Daytona intends to give 30 days' notice for a material reduction of a generally available feature and will use commercially reasonable efforts to keep backwards compatibility for 12 months after an Update.

source.quote: We reserve the right to modify fees and may do so by posting such modification on the Services or informing you through other reasonable methods.

facts.label: Support
facts.value: Community Slack on every plan; private Slack and ticket support on Team and Enterprise; custom support SLAs on Enterprise. No published response time.

well: A coding agent that needs a real kernel: every sandbox is a Firecracker VM, and Docker runs when the image ships it.
A short, untrusted task: 0.125-core granularity, per-second billing, free ephemeral disk and $200 of credit make a ten-minute run cost cents.
A browser or computer-use agent: Chromium is in the standard image, the VNC desktop ships with the runtime, and Computer Use is an API.
A team that needs projects, roles and a dollar budget: each product gets its own project, key and monthly cap.
A macOS or Windows build: a real M4 Pro Mac reservation with Xcode, or a Windows VM, next to the Linux fleet.
badly: A personal assistant that must stay on for weeks: the 24- or 48-hour session cap deletes it, and Linux cannot stop or pause.
A workload that expects its disk between short sessions: the sandbox disk is ephemeral, and persistence means a volume at $0.000108/GiB-hour.
A GPU workload today: the 2.0 GPU page says coming soon.
An EU-only workload: no European region is documented.
A team of five on Starter: three members, so Team is $250 a month before compute.
An always-on Discord bot, n8n instance or MCP server: no scheduler, no wake-on-request, and a 24-hour recreate changes the preview URL.

usability.dashboard: Yes: sandboxes, images, snapshots, volumes, projects, keys and billing, with Terminal, Files, Desktop and SSH tabs on a sandbox, plus a TypeScript Playground that runs SDK code in the browser.
usability.withoutCode: Partly. The dashboard creates a sandbox and opens a terminal or desktop in one click, but every documented agent setup is a command or a script, and the Playground is TypeScript.
usability.signup: Create an account at app.daytona.com; no card is needed, and Starter includes a $200 one-time credit. Team is $250 a month and needs a payment method; a pre-paid organisation must add one before the change.
usability.docs: Every docs page has a Markdown twin at the same URL with .md, an llms.txt index and a 1.8 MB llms-full.txt bundle. Python and TypeScript SDK references, a CLI reference, an OpenAPI reference and 27 guides. Support is community Slack on every plan, private Slack and tickets on Team, custom SLAs on Enterprise.
tripsUp: Every Linux sandbox is deleted at 24 hours on Starter or 48 on Team; there is no stop, pause or keep-alive.
The disk is ephemeral. Files between sessions need a volume, which bills from the first GiB at $0.000108.
The pricing page opens on the Preemptible tab; on-demand is 43% more, and spot can be reclaimed without warning.
The standard preview token opens every private port on the sandbox and never expires.
The agent guides still use 1.x --snapshot and --auto-stop flags, and the default image's contents are unpublished.
No EU region is documented, and the 300-second platform default timeout is described as conditional.

caveats.issue: The size ceiling is three different numbers
caveats.detail: The docs cap a Linux sandbox at 16 cores, 32 GiB and 256 GiB; the same docs cap Starter at 4 cores and 16 GiB and Team at 8 and 32; the price list advertises 64 cores, 128 GiB and 512 GiB to 3 TiB for both plans. The limits page is the one that describes the 400 a create returns, so treat 4 and 8 cores as real and the price table as an Enterprise copy — but a buyer comparing the two pages will think Starter is eight times larger than it is.

evidence.quote: A Linux sandbox may guarantee at most 16 cores, 32GiB memory, and 256GiB disk.

caveats.issue: A persistent Linux sandbox is required for snapshots but never defined
caveats.detail: The lifecycle table gives Linux no stop, pause or fork and no filesystem persistence, yet the snapshot page says only a persistent sandbox or a warm template can be captured, and migration imports v0 sandboxes as persistent ones. Nothing says how to create or recognise a persistent Linux sandbox, so a reader cannot tell in advance whether their sandbox can be snapshotted.

caveats.issue: Linux has no stop or pause, yet the pricing FAQ says a stopped sandbox keeps its state and costs nothing
caveats.detail: The FAQ answers the obvious cost question with 'a stopped or paused sandbox keeps its state and is not metered'. On Linux there is no stop or pause to use: the sandbox bills its guarantee until it is deleted at the 24- or 48-hour cap. On macOS, stopping does not stop the Mac reservation. Only Windows matches the FAQ.

evidence.quote: No. CPU and memory are billed only while a sandbox is running, and ephemeral NVMe disk is free. A stopped or paused sandbox keeps its state and is not metered. Volumes are billed separately.

caveats.issue: Windows and GPU are sold while their own pages say coming soon
caveats.detail: The price list sells Windows core licences, nine GPU models and GPU plan limits, and the lifecycle and preemption pages describe both classes. Their dedicated doc pages are placeholders that say coming soon. Assume both exist — the price list is the more specific document — but expect to learn the details from presets and the dashboard rather than a page.

caveats.issue: Preemptible GPU prices are published, but GPU sandboxes cannot be spot
caveats.detail: The price list has a Preemptible column for every GPU model and the page opens on that tab. The preemption page says GPU sandboxes cannot be spot. The preemptible column is 1.x legacy: a GPU workload pays the on-demand column, 30% to 70% more than the tab suggests.

evidence.quote: GPU sandboxes cannot be spot, so GPU experiments run at full price.

caveats.issue: macOS is 'not metered' but has a core-hour rate, and a stopped Mac keeps paying
caveats.detail: Billing says macOS sandboxes are not metered and their Mac reservation is charged instead; the price list still prints a macOS core-hour rate. The reservation is the real price ($2.5032 a Mac-hour, $60.08 a day, charged when a period starts and not refunded when it ends early), so a stopped macOS sandbox is not free even though billing says stopped sandboxes are not metered.

caveats.issue: The 300-second platform timeout is conditional, and the cap is 24 hours
caveats.detail: The docs say Daytona applies a 300-second platform default 'if the platform default is enabled' and never say whether it is; the projects example sets 1,800 seconds and a 600-second idle timeout. A sandbox created without an explicit timeout therefore lives somewhere between five minutes and 24 hours, and is deleted at the cap with no stop in between. Set a timeout on every create.

evidence.quote: Daytona applies the platform default timeout of 300 seconds, if the platform default is enabled.
"ephemeral": { "timeout_seconds": 1800, "idle_timeout_seconds": 600 }

strengths: A real microVM per sandbox: Firecracker Linux, Cloud Hypervisor Windows and GPU, Apple Virtualization macOS, each with its own kernel.
Custom sizes from 0.125 to 16 cores, billed per second with a guaranteed floor and free ephemeral NVMe.
A desktop stack and Computer Use API that ship with the runtime, plus Chromium in the standard image.
Projects, seventeen roles and dollar budgets as first-class objects, with project-scoped keys and scopes.
Linux, Windows and macOS from one API, with native M4 Pro Mac reservations for Xcode work.
$200 of free compute with no card, and spot at 30% off for interruptible work.
